headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways between Langflow and oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Langflow reads/writes server files and can ingest uploaded files; oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and can access AGENTS.md/README.md. A shared workspace or file bridge lets one agent’s content influence the other, so prompt injection is plausible in default-ish deployments. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace or repo files
IF either agent treats file contents as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic instruction parsing from shared files
Require provenance tags on imported content
Restrict file access to read-only for one side
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering

B_data_leakage.rationale: Langflow handles flow inputs, intermediate outputs, uploaded files, and stored secrets; oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data, and both have broad network egress. If they share files or credentials, sensitive data can be exposed or forwarded externally by either agent. This is a default-dangerous pathway with irreversible exfiltration potential.
conditions: IF the two agents share a filesystem, config directory, or credential store
IF either agent is configured to send file contents or session history to external APIs
mitigations: Isolate credentials per agent
Mount separate workspaces
Turn off uploads for sensitive projects
Review outbound API destinations
requires-engineering: enforce DLP and egress allowlists

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Langflow can write the server filesystem and spawn subprocesses; oh-my-openagent can also spawn subprocesses and uses full-permissions mode. With shared mutable paths, both can race on the same files or configs, and neither profile shows locking. The overlap is enough to make destructive conflicts plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory or config files
IF no external lock or coordinator serializes writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Run one agent at a time
Make shared files read-only
Back up mutable state before runs
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow is a graph-based orchestrator that can chain multiple agents, while oh-my-openagent exposes task/message actions and LSP operations. If Langflow feeds outputs into oh-my-openagent without verification, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or code changes. The pair’s interaction is plausible and dangerous, though not directly sandbox-validated.
conditions: IF Langflow output is passed into oh-my-openagent tasks or messages
IF no human or programmatic verification step checks the intermediate output
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require human approval for actions
Limit oh-my-openagent to read-only tasks
Log and diff intermediate outputs
requires-engineering: add schema validation and confidence gating

E_compliance.rationale: Langflow stores per-flow credentials and handles uploaded files, while oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, and provider auth data. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if regulated data flows through both. I cite both because the risk arises from their combined handling of different data classes.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed in Langflow flows
IF oh-my-openagent stores or transmits that data under different retention or residency rules
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared flows
Separate retention policies by agent
Document data residency for each service
Purge session history after use
requires-engineering: align compliance controls and audit logging
